I stopped asking Claude, “What digital product should I create?” Because that was giving me the same generic ideas anyone could come up with. Instead, I started giving it the information it actually needed to figure out what my audience would buy. Here’s the prompt: “I want to create a digital product, but I don’t want you to give me generic product ideas. I want you to help me identify what my audience is already telling me they need. My niche is: [YOUR NICHE] My audience is: [WHO YOU HELP] They come to me for: [WHAT YOU’RE KNOWN FOR] The questions I get asked most are: [QUESTIONS] The problems they talk about most are: [PROBLEMS] My best-performing content is usually about: [TOPICS]. Based on this, identify the 5 most specific problems my audience would realistically pay to solve. For each one, tell me: what they’re struggling with; the result they actually want; a simple digital product that could help them get that result; why this is stronger than a generic product idea. Then rank all 5 from strongest to weakest based on urgency, specificity and how easy the result is to understand. Do not build the product yet. Help me choose the right problem first.” That last line matters. I don’t want Claude creating a 47-page ebook just because I told it to make me something. I want it to help me figure out what people actually want first. Then I build. That’s the difference. Save this and try it before you create your next digital product.
